allosaurus:enwiki:3.title: Allosaurus (Initial finds and naming of Allosaurus)

allosaurus:enwiki:4.title: Allosaurus (Renaming to Antrodemus and early discoveries at Dinosaur National Monument)

facts.statement: The first definitive fossil remains of Allosaurus were described in 1877 by Othniel C. Marsh.
facts.quote: The first fossil remains that could definitively be ascribed to this genus were described in 1877 by Othniel C. Marsh.

facts.statement: Marsh named the genus Allosaurus, meaning "different lizard", because he believed its vertebrae were uniquely lightweight.
facts.quote: The name "Allosaurus" means "different lizard", alluding to its lightweight vertebrae, which Marsh believed were unique.

facts.statement: Most Allosaurus fossils come from the Morrison Formation in North America, with additional finds in Portugal.
facts.quote: The bulk of Allosaurus remains come from North America's Morrison Formation, with material also known from the Alcobaça, Bombarral, and Lourinhã formations in Portugal.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was known as Antrodemus for over half the 20th century until studies of Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry remains restored its name.
facts.quote: It was known for over half of the 20th century as Antrodemus, but a study of the abundant remains from the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry returned the name "Allosaurus" to prominence.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was a large bipedal predator with a light, robust skull containing dozens of sharp, serrated teeth.
facts.quote: Allosaurus was a large bipedal predator for its time. Its skull was light, robust, and equipped with dozens of sharp, serrated teeth.

facts.statement: A. fragilis averaged 7.5 to 8 meters in length, with the largest specimens estimated at 9 meters.
facts.quote: It averaged 7.5-8 m in length for A. fragilis, with the largest specimens of A. fragilis estimated as being 9 m long.

facts.statement: Allosaurus had small three-fingered hands relative to its powerful legs and a long, muscular tail for balance.
facts.quote: Relative to the large and powerful legs, its three-fingered hands were small and the body was balanced by a long, muscular tail.

facts.statement: Allosaurus is classified within the family Allosauridae.
facts.quote: It is classified in the family Allosauridae.

facts.statement: As the most abundant large predator in the Morrison Formation, Allosaurus was an apex predator likely hunting ornithopods, stegosaurids, and sauropods.
facts.quote: As the most abundant large predator of the Morrison Formation, Allosaurus was an apex predator of the food chain and probably preyed on large herbivorous dinosaurs such as ornithopods, stegosaurids, and sauropods.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was discovered during the "Bone Wars," a rivalry between Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope that spurred fossil discoveries in the Western US.
facts.quote: Allosaurus was discovered during the Bone Wars, a feud between two American paleontologists, Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope, that led to a surge of fossil discoveries in the Western US.

facts.statement: The first fossil in Allosaurus's taxonomic history was a bone obtained secondhand by Ferdinand V. Hayden in 1869.
facts.quote: The first described fossil in the taxonomic history of Allosaurus was a bone obtained secondhand by Ferdinand V. Hayden in 1869.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy initially identified the first Allosaurus fossil as belonging to the genus Antrodemus.
facts.quote: He later decided it deserved its own genus, Antrodemus.

facts.statement: Othniel C. Marsh named the type species Allosaurus fragilis in 1877.
facts.quote: Marsh gave these remains the name Allosaurus fragilis in 1877.

facts.statement: The original Allosaurus fossils were uncovered by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel W. Williston in autumn 1877 at Felch Quarry, Colorado.
facts.quote: The bones were uncovered by two of Marsh's collectors, Benjamin Mudge and Samuel W. Williston, in the autumn of 1877 at Felch Quarry, in the Garden Park area of Colorado.

facts.statement: Marsh hired Marshall P. Felch in 1883 to continue excavations at Felch Quarry.
facts.quote: In 1883, Marsh hired the original discoverer of the quarry, Marshall P. Felch, to continue excavations.

facts.statement: Excavations at Felch Quarry yielded a mostly complete Allosaurus skeleton (USNM 4734) that later became the neotype specimen for A. fragilis.
facts.quote: Felch's subsequent discoveries made the quarry one of the prime sites of the Morrison, and included the holotype specimens of Ceratosaurus nasicornis, Stegosaurus stenops, and a mostly complete Allosaurus skeleton (USNM 4734) that would later be selected as the neotype specimen of Allosaurus fragilis (the single specimen the species is based on, replacing the inadequate holotype).

facts.statement: Antrodemus was the accepted name for over 50 years until James H. Madsen argued that Allosaurus should be used due to the poor quality of Antrodemus's diagnostic material.
facts.quote: Antrodemus became the accepted name for this familiar genus for over 50 years, until James H. Madsen published on the Cleveland-Lloyd specimens and concluded that Allosaurus should be used because Antrodemus was based on material with poor, if any, diagnostic features and locality information.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass discovered the site that became Dinosaur National Monument in Utah in 1909.
facts.quote: In 1909, Earl Douglass from the Carnegie Museum discovered what should later become Dinosaur National Monument in Utah.

facts.statement: Douglass and his team excavated over 700,000 pounds of fossils, including several Allosaurus specimens, from a single quarry until 2022.
facts.quote: Until 2022, Douglass and his team excavated over 700,000 lbs of fossils of multiple dinosaur species from a single quarry, including several Allosaurus specimens.

facts.statement: Specimen CM 11844, collected between 1913 and 1915, includes much of an Allosaurus skeleton and a fragmentary skull.
facts.quote: Among these finds is CM 11844, which was collected between 1913 and 1915 and comprises much of the skeleton and a fragmentary skull.

facts.statement: The University of Utah uncovered specimen DINO 2560 in summer 1924, which was the best-preserved Allosaurus known at that time.
facts.quote: During the summer of 1924, the University of Utah uncovered DINO 2560, the best preserved Allosaurus specimen known at that time.

facts.statement: Major fossil excavations at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah did not begin until 1960.
facts.quote: major operations did not begin there until 1960.

facts.statement: The Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry preserves fossils of at least 73 individual dinosaurs, including a minimum of 46 Allosaurus fragilis.
facts.quote: the quarry preserves a minimum of 73 individual dinosaurs and at least 46 of those are A. fragilis.

facts.statement: Allosaurus individuals found at the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry range in size from less than 1 meter to 12 meters in length.
facts.quote: Skeletal remains from the quarry pertain to individuals of almost all ages and sizes, from less than 1 m to 12 m long.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was officially designated as the state fossil of Utah in 1988.
facts.quote: Allosaurus was designated as the state fossil of Utah in 1988.

facts.statement: A nearly complete 95% articulated Allosaurus specimen known as "Big Al" was discovered in 1991.
facts.quote: they discovered "Big Al" (MOR 693) in 1991: a 95% complete, partially articulated Allosaurus specimen.

facts.statement: The "Big Al" specimen was a subadult estimated to be only 87% of its full adult size.
facts.quote: This was below the average size for Allosaurus, as it was a subadult estimated at only 87% grown.

facts.statement: Statistical analyses between 1996 and 1999 suggested that variations in Allosaurus fossils from the Morrison Formation represent individual differences rather than distinct species.
facts.quote: a series of statistical analyses by David K. Smith between 1996 and 1999 suggested that the differences seen in the Morrison Formation material can be attributed to individual variation.

facts.statement: The validity of the European species Allosaurus europaeus has been debated, with some studies suggesting it is a synonym of A. fragilis, a doubtful name, or requires re-evaluation.
facts.quote: The status of A. europaeus was controversially discussed in the subsequent years, with different studies arguing that the species is a synonym of A. fragilis, a nomen dubium (doubtful name), or in need of re-evaluation.

facts.statement: The species Allosaurus jimmadseni was formally described in 2020 after previously being an invalid name.
facts.quote: Chure and Mark Loewen formally described the species in 2020.

facts.statement: The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature ratified a petition in December 2023 to designate specimen USNM 4734 as the neotype for Allosaurus fragilis.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul and Kenneth Carpenter submitted a petition to the ICZN in 2010 to have the more complete specimen USNM 4734 selected as a neotype, a decision that was ratified by the ICZN on December 29, 2023.

facts.statement: A 2024 study suggested that the holotype of Saurophaganax is a fossil chimera mixing Allosaurus and sauropod bones.
facts.quote: A 2024 reassessment by Andy Danison and colleagues suggested that the Saurophaganax specimen is a chimera that combines the bones of Allosaurus with those of a sauropod.

facts.statement: Analysis of the Saurophaganax specimen revealed distinct Allosaurus bones that warranted the creation of the new species Allosaurus anax.
facts.quote: The Allosaurus bones, however, were found to be distinct enough to warrant a new species of Allosaurus, A. anax.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was a large theropod characterized by a massive skull, short neck, long tail, and reduced forelimbs.
facts.quote: Allosaurus was a typical large theropod, having a massive skull on a short neck, a long, slightly sloping tail, and reduced forelimbs.

facts.statement: The best-known species, A. fragilis, is estimated to have been 7 to 9 meters long and weighed between 1.7 and 2.7 metric tons.
facts.quote: The size of A. fragilis, the best-known species, has been estimated at 7-9 m and its mass at 1.7-2.7 MT.

facts.statement: A large specimen once classified as Saurophaganax was estimated to reach 10.5 meters in length and was sometimes included in Allosaurus as A. maximus.
facts.quote: The dubious genus Saurophaganax (OMNH 1708) was estimated to reach around 10.5 m in length, and its single species has sometimes been included in the genus Allosaurus as A. maximus.

facts.statement: A computational study estimated the optimal body mass for Allosaurus to be 2.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: A separate computational project estimated the adaptive optimum body mass in Allosaurus to be 2.3 MT.

facts.statement: The European species A. europaeus has been measured up to 6 to 8 meters in length and 1 metric ton in body mass.
facts.quote: A. europaeus has been measured up to 6 - 8 m in length and 1 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Allosaurus had a light skull equipped with dozens of sharp, serrated teeth that were modestly proportioned for its size.
facts.quote: The skull of Allosaurus was light and equipped with dozens of sharp, serrated teeth, and both were modestly proportioned for a theropod of its size.

facts.statement: Allosaurus possessed a pair of horns formed by lacrimal bones extending above and in front of the eyes, which varied in shape and size.
facts.quote: The lacrimal bones of Allosaurus extend above and in front of the eyes to form a pair of horns which varied in shape and size.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the horns of Allosaurus were likely covered in keratin and may have served as sunshades, for display, or in combat, though they were fragile.
facts.quote: The horns were probably covered in a keratin sheath and may have had a variety of functions, including acting as sunshades for the eyes, being used for display, and being used in combat against other members of the same species (although they were fragile).

facts.statement: Allosaurus had joints in its skull and lower jaws that allowed them to bow outward, increasing the animal's gape.
facts.quote: The skull and lower jaws had joints that permitted motion within these units. In the lower jaws, the bones of the front and back halves loosely articulated, permitting the jaws to bow outward and increasing the animal's gape.

facts.statement: Allosaurus had nine neck vertebrae, 14 back vertebrae, and five sacral vertebrae supporting the hips.
facts.quote: Allosaurus has nine vertebrae in the neck, 14 in the back, and five in the sacrum supporting the hips.

facts.statement: Allosaurus forelimbs were short, about 35% the length of the hindlimbs in adults, and ended in three fingers with large, curved claws.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Allosaurus are short in comparison to the hindlimbs (only about 35% the length of the hindlimbs in adults) and have three fingers per hand, tipped with large, strongly curved and pointed claws.

facts.statement: The innermost finger of Allosaurus was the largest and diverged from the others, with a phalangeal formula of 2-3-4-0-0.
facts.quote: The innermost (or thumb) is the largest, and diverged from the others. The phalangeal formula is 2-3-4-0-0, meaning that the innermost digit has two bones, the next has three, and the third finger has four.

facts.statement: Studies suggest that variation in Allosaurus skulls was likely due to individual differences rather than multiple species.
facts.quote: A later study by Smith incorporating specimens from the Garden Park and Dinosaur National Monument sites found no justification for multiple species based on skeletal variation; skull variation was most common and was gradational, suggesting individual variation was responsible.

facts.statement: It is debated whether several gigantic specimens attributed to Allosaurus actually belong to other genera.
facts.quote: Several gigantic specimens have been attributed to Allosaurus, but may in fact belong to other genera.

facts.statement: The body mass of the species Allosaurus anax is estimated at 3.8 to 4.6 metric tons, though this is based on fragmentary material.
facts.quote: The body mass of this species was estimated around 3.8 - 4.6 MT based on fragmentary material.

facts.statement: Madsen suggested that unfused pubic bones in Allosaurus might indicate sexual dimorphism to facilitate egg-laying, but this proposal has not gained further support.
facts.quote: Madsen noted that in about half of the individuals from the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry, independent of size, the pubes had not fused to each other at their foot ends. He suggested that this was a sexual characteristic, with females lacking fused bones to make egg-laying easier. This proposal has not attracted further attention, however.

facts.statement: A skin impression from a juvenile Allosaurus measuring 30 square centimeters was found on the anterior dorsal ribs and pectoral region.
facts.quote: One impression, from a juvenile specimen, measures 30 square centimeters and is associated with the anterior dorsal ribs/pectoral region.

facts.statement: A skin impression from the base of the tail of the "Big Al Two" specimen measures 20 by 20 centimeters and contains scales up to 2 centimeters in diameter.
facts.quote: A skin impression from the "Big Al Two" specimen, associated with the base of the tail, measures 20 centimeters by 20 centimeters and shows large scales measuring up to 2 centimeters in diameter.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the large tail scales of the "Big Al Two" specimen might belong to a sauropod rather than Allosaurus due to the presence of non-theropod remains at the site.
facts.quote: However, it has been noted that these scales are more similar to those of sauropods, and due to the presence of non-theropod remains associated with the tail of "Big Al Two" there is a possibility that this skin impression is not from Allosaurus.

facts.statement: A single Allosaurus fossil preserves a 20 by 20 centimeter skin impression from the ventral neck containing scutate scales 0.5 centimeters wide and 11 centimeters long.
facts.quote: The same fossil also preserves skin measuring 20 by 20 centimeters from the ventral side of the neck, showing scutate scales measuring 0.5 centimeters wide and 11 centimeters long.

facts.statement: Crushed eggs found in Colorado have been suggested to belong to Allosaurus, indicating the animal laid eggs.
facts.quote: Remains may reach as far back in the lifespan as eggs—crushed eggs from Colorado have been suggested as those of Allosaurus.

facts.statement: Histological analysis suggests Allosaurus stopped growing at around 22 to 28 years of age, similar to other large theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Based on histological analysis of limb bones, bone deposition appears to stop at around 22 to 28 years, which is comparable to that of other large theropods like Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Analysis indicates Allosaurus grew fastest at age 15, gaining approximately 148 kilograms (326 lb) per year.
facts.quote: From the same analysis, its maximum growth appears to have been at age 15, with an estimated growth rate of about 148 kilograms (326 lb) per year.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the medullary bone found in a Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry Allosaurus specimen indicates it was a female or if it resulted from bone pathology.
facts.quote: However, other studies have called into question some cases of medullary bone in dinosaurs, including this Allosaurus individual. Data from extant birds suggested that the medullary bone in this Allosaurus individual may have been the result of a bone pathology instead.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests juvenile Allosaurus were faster cursorial predators of small prey, while adults became ambush hunters of large prey.
facts.quote: These differences suggest that like the much later-living tyrannosaurids, younger Allosaurus were faster and filled separate predatory niches than adults, perhaps being cursorial predators of smaller prey as juveniles before becoming ambush hunters of large prey as they matured.

facts.statement: Allosaurus skull bones grew isometrically, increasing in size without changing their proportions.
facts.quote: The skull bones appear to have generally grown isometrically, increasing in size without changing in proportion.

facts.statement: Robert T. Bakker compared Allosaurus to Cenozoic saber-toothed mammals, noting adaptations like reduced jaw muscles, increased neck muscles, and the ability to open jaws extremely wide.
facts.quote: Robert T. Bakker, comparing Allosaurus to Cenozoic saber-toothed carnivorous mammals, found similar adaptations, such as a reduction of jaw muscles and increase in neck muscles, and the ability to open the jaws extremely wide.

facts.statement: Studies by Stephen Lautenschager et al. indicate Allosaurus could open its jaws to a maximum 92-degree angle, a wider gape than Tyrannosaurus or Erlikosaurus, while sustaining considerable muscle force.
facts.quote: Studies done by Stephen Lautenschager et al. from the University of Bristol also indicate Allosaurus could open its jaws quite wide and sustain considerable muscle force. When compared with Tyrannosaurus and the therizinosaurid Erlikosaurus in the same study, it was found that Allosaurus had a wider gape than either; the animal was capable of opening its jaws to a 92-degree angle at maximum.

facts.statement: Research suggests Allosaurus may have gripped prey with its skull and feet to pull back and up and remove flesh, differing from tyrannosaurids which likely used lateral skull shakes similar to crocodilians.
facts.quote: The animal could have gripped prey with the skull and feet, then pulled back and up to remove flesh. This differs from the prey-handling envisioned for tyrannosaurids, which probably tore flesh with lateral shakes of the skull, similar to crocodilians.

facts.statement: One hypothesis suggests Allosaurus acted as a "flesh grazer," taking bites from living sauropods sufficient to sustain itself without needing to kill the prey outright.
facts.quote: Another possibility for handling large prey is that theropods like Allosaurus were "flesh grazers" which could take bites of flesh out of living sauropods that were sufficient to sustain the predator so it would not have needed to expend the effort to kill the prey outright.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Allosaurus forelimbs were strong enough to restrain prey, compatible with hypotheses of throat-crushing attacks similar to modern big cats.
facts.quote: This is compatible with other evidence that the forelimbs were strong and capable of restraining prey.

facts.statement: Research deems the "hatchet jaw" attack unlikely, reinterpreting the wide gape as an adaptation for delivering muscle-driven bites to large prey, with weaker jaw muscles being a trade-off for the widened gape.
facts.quote: A paper on the cranio-dental morphology of Allosaurus and how it worked has deemed the hatchet jaw attack unlikely, reinterpreting the unusually wide gape as an adaptation to allow Allosaurus to deliver a muscle-driven bite to large prey, with the weaker jaw muscles being a trade-off to allow for the widened gape.

facts.statement: Since the 1970s, researchers have speculated that Allosaurus hunted large prey like sauropods in groups.
facts.quote: It has been speculated since the 1970s that Allosaurus preyed on sauropods and other large dinosaurs by hunting in groups.

facts.statement: Evidence for cannibalism in Allosaurus includes shed teeth found among rib fragments and tooth marks on shoulder blades.
facts.quote: There is some evidence for cannibalism in Allosaurus, including Allosaurus shed teeth found among rib fragments, possible tooth marks on a shoulder blade, and cannibalized allosaur skeletons among the bones at Bakker's lair sites.

facts.statement: CT scans of an Allosaurus endocast show its brain structure was more similar to crocodilians than to birds or other living archosaurs.
facts.quote: The brain of Allosaurus, as interpreted from spiral CT scanning of an endocast, was more consistent with crocodilian brains than those of the other living archosaurs, birds.

facts.statement: The vestibular apparatus structure indicates that the Allosaurus skull was held nearly horizontal.
facts.quote: The structure of the vestibular apparatus indicates that the skull was held nearly horizontal, as opposed to strongly tipped up or down.

facts.statement: The Allosaurus inner ear structure suggests it was adapted to hear lower frequencies and had difficulty hearing subtle sounds.
facts.quote: The structure of the inner ear was like that of a crocodilian, indicating that Allosaurus was more adapted to hear lower frequencies and would have had difficulty hearing subtle sounds.

facts.statement: Allosaurus had large olfactory bulbs well suited for detecting odors, which were typical for an animal of its size.
facts.quote: The olfactory bulbs were large and well suited for detecting odors, but were typical for an animal of its size.

facts.statement: The relatively small opening for the trigeminal nerve in Allosaurus suggests it lacked the heightened facial sensitivity found in crocodilians and some birds.
facts.quote: The opening for the trigeminal nerve was relatively small compared to those of birds and crocodilians; this is also true of other non-avian theropods, and suggests they did not have the heightened facial sensitivity of crocodilians and some birds.

facts.statement: Allosaurus had a proportionally greater endocranial volume than smaller theropods, likely to accommodate larger dural venous sinuses for brain cooling.
facts.quote: As with other large theropods, the endocranial volume of Allosaurus is proportionally greater than in smaller theropods; this is thought to have accommodated larger dural venous sinuses, helping to cool the brain.

facts.statement: In 1972, Kristen Petersen and colleagues documented pathologies in Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry specimens, including rib fractures, joint stiffness, fused tail vertebrae, and possible bite-induced bone amputations.
facts.quote: In 1972, Kristen Petersen and colleagues listed multiple pathologies present in specimens from the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry. These include willow breaks in two ribs, distortion of joint surfaces, ankylosis (joint stiffness) in tail vertebrae, instances were vertebrae from the tip of the tail are fused together, the amputation of a chevron and a foot bone possibly due to bites, exostoses (bony outgrowths) in a toe bone, and lesions that are possibly caused by infections.

facts.statement: A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues found stress fractures in 3 of 47 hand bones and 17 of 281 foot bones in Allosaurus, a higher rate than in Albertosaurus, Ornithomimus, and Archaeornithomimus.
facts.quote: In a 2001 study, Bruce Rothschild and colleagues reported stress fractures in 3 out of 47 examined hand bones and in 17 out of 281 examined foot bones of Allosaurus, more than in Albertosaurus, Ornithomimus and Archaeornithomimus.

facts.statement: Researchers identified two cases of tendon avulsions in the forelimbs of Allosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: The authors also identified two cases of tendon avulsions, where parts of the bone was torn out by an attaching tendon, in forelimbs of Allosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: The specimen known as "Big Al" preserves 19 distinct pathologies across its skeleton.
facts.quote: The specimen "Big Al" preserves 19 pathologies across the skeleton.

facts.statement: In "Big Al", a chronic infection in the right foot caused the first bone of the middle toe to swell and push against the outer toes.
facts.quote: In the right foot, the first bone of the middle toe is greatly swollen due to a chronic infection (osteomyelitis), causing it to push against the outer toes.

facts.statement: The specimen "Big Al II" exhibits multiple pathologies in the lower jaw, vertebrae, ribs, shoulder blade, humerus, toe bones, and pelvis.
facts.quote: The specimen "Big Al II" also shows multiple pathologies, including in the lower jaw, in several vertebrae and ribs, in the left shoulder blade and the left humerus, in two left toe bones, and in the right ischium of the pelvis.

facts.statement: Christian Foth and colleagues suggested in 2015 that pathologies in the left shoulder blade and ribs of "Big Al II" resulted from a single impact.
facts.quote: According to Christian Foth and colleagues in 2015, the pathologies in the shoulder blade and ribs, all on the left side of the body, could have been caused by a single impact to the body.

facts.statement: Lida Xing and colleagues described specimen HS0387 from Dana Quarry in 2022, noting it held the first evidence of spondyloarthropathy in a theropod.
facts.quote: Another specimen with multiple pathologies (HS0387) from Dana Quarry in Wyoming was described by Lida Xing and colleagues in 2022. Pathologies in the right shoulder blade and in the eighth and ninth dorsal vertebrae of this specimen were interpreted as spondyloarthropathy, the first evidence for this condition in a theropod.

facts.statement: Allosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Both the North American and European occurrences date to the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: Fossils of Allosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation of the American West and in formations in Portugal.
facts.quote: Allosaurus is known from the Morrison Formation of the American West and from the Alcobaça, Bombarral, and Lourinhã formations in Portugal.

facts.statement: Specimens previously assigned to Allosaurus from Russia, Tanzania, and Switzerland are no longer classified within the genus.
facts.quote: Allosaurus has also been reported from several other countries such as Russia (A. sibiricus), Tanzania (A. tendagurensis), and Switzerland (A. meriani), though these specimens are no longer assigned to the genus.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was the most common theropod in the Morrison Formation, making up 70 to 75% of theropod specimens found there.
facts.quote: Allosaurus is the most common theropod in the Morrison Formation, accounting for 70 to 75% of theropod specimens.

facts.statement: Isotopic evidence suggests Allosaurus was an opportunistic predator that consumed Camarasaurus, Camptosaurus, and Diplodocus, though it is unclear whether it hunted or scavenged them.
facts.quote: Calcium isotopic values show Allosaurus was an opportunistic predator that ate Camarasaurus, Camptosaurus, and Diplodocus, although it is unclear if it was hunting or scavenging on the sauropods.

facts.statement: Allosaurus primarily consumed flesh and ate only small amounts of bone, unlike tyrannosaurids such as Tyrannosaurus which consumed more bone.
facts.quote: It also revealed Allosaurus primarily consumed flesh with only small amounts of bone being consumed compared to tyrannosaurids like Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Allosaurus was a compact, fast but less maneuverable predator that likely preferred dry floodplain environments.
facts.quote: Allosaurus was more compact, with longer legs, faster but less maneuverable, and seems to have preferred dry floodplains.

facts.statement: About 66% of the vertebrate fossils in Utah's Cleveland-Lloyd quarry belong to the single species Allosaurus fragilis, and the bones are disarticulated and well-mixed.
facts.quote: Utah's Cleveland-Lloyd quarry is unusual in that about 66% of the vertebrate fossils belong to a single species of carnivore, A. fragilis, and that the bones are disarticulated (no longer connected to each other) and well-mixed.

facts.statement: Bite marks found on Allosaurus fossils suggest scavenging by other theropods or by other Allosaurus individuals.
facts.quote: bite marks found on Allosaurus material suggest scavenging, either from the other theropods or from another Allosaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Allosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1877

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Allosaurus is Allosaurus fragilis.
facts.quote: type_species: Allosaurus fragilis

facts.statement: The genus Allosaurus includes subdivisions such as A. europaeus, A. jimmadseni, and A. anax.
facts.quote: subdivision: Allosaurus europaeus Mateus, Walen & Antunes, 2006 Allosaurus jimmadseni Chure and Loewen, 2020 Allosaurus anax Danison et al., 2024

facts.statement: A 2024 study suggests that A. fragilis and A. jimmadseni were contemporaneous but geographically separated, with A. fragilis in the south and east and A. jimmadseni in the north and west of the Morrison basin.
facts.quote: According to a 2024 study by Susannah Maidment, A. fragilis and A. jimmadseni appear to have been contemporaneous but separated geographically, with A. fragilis concentrated in the south and east of the Morrison basin and A. jimmadseni in the north and west.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Allosaurus hunted or scavenged sauropods like Camarasaurus and Diplodocus.
facts.quote: It is unclear if it was hunting or scavenging on the sauropods.

facts.statement: A popular hypothesis suggests the Cleveland-Lloyd quarry was a predator trap where Allosaurus became mired.
facts.quote: A popular idea is that the site was a predator trap to which the Allosaurus were attracted and became mired.

facts.statement: Some studies propose that a severe drought caused an Allosaurus population to congregate around a water hole, deterring other dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Other studies postulated a single catastrophe as the cause, such as a severe drought during which an Allosaurus population congregated around a water hole and, by their presence, deterred other dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Allosaurus is an extinct genus of allosaurid theropod dinosaur with three or possibly four valid species.
facts.quote: Allosaurus (gr. "lagarto extraño") es un género extinto con tres posiblemente cuatro especies válidas de dinosaurio terópodo alosáurido

facts.statement: Allosaurus lived during the late Jurassic period, between 155 and 145 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivieron a finales de la época Jurásico Superior, entre 155 a 145 millones de años, entre el Oxfordiano y el Titoniano

facts.statement: Fossils of Allosaurus have been found in what is now North America and Europe.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy es Norteamérica y Europa

facts.statement: The type fossils of Allosaurus were described in 1877 by paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh.
facts.quote: Los fósiles tipo fueron descritos en 1877 por el paleontólogo Othniel Charles Marsh

facts.statement: Allosaurus was a bipedal carnivore with robust legs and claws, balanced by a heavy tail.
facts.quote: Era un carnívoro bípedo con garras y patas robustas, equilibradas por su pesada cola

facts.statement: Allosaurus had a curved skull with serrated teeth and low, irregular crests above and in front of the eyes.
facts.quote: Su cráneo curvo provisto de dientes aserrados poseía además unas crestas bajas irregulares, sobre y delante de los ojos

facts.statement: Despite being a large predator, Allosaurus weighed about as much as a modern Indian rhinoceros.
facts.quote: no pesaba tanto, siendo comparable en masa a un moderno rinoceronte indio

facts.statement: The high number of Allosaurus found at single sites suggests they may have lived in groups.
facts.quote: El gran número de Allosaurus encontrado en un mismo sitio hace pensar que tenían una cierta vida en grupo

facts.statement: Allosaurus was the most common large predator in North America and one of the most abundant carnivorous dinosaurs in the fossil record, with nearly 60 specimens known.
facts.quote: Fue el depredador grande más común en lo que hoy es Norteamérica, de hecho es famoso por ser el dinosaurio carnívoro más abundante y común en el registro fósil con cerca de 60 especímenes

facts.statement: The well-preserved adult specimen USNM 4734 of Allosaurus fragilis shows fused scapulae and coracoids, as well as fused sacral vertebrae, indicating adulthood.
facts.quote: Allosaurus fragilis, la especie mejor conocida, presenta un individuo adulto muy bien preservado, USNM 4734, con las escápulas firmemente fusionadas con sus coracoides, y todas las vértebras sacras fusionadas, ambos signos de adultez en dinosaurios

facts.statement: The specimen AMNH 680, which has the largest known femur at 973 millimeters long, may have weighed over 2.65 tons and reached a length of up to 9.7 meters.
facts.quote: El ejemplar con el mayor fémur conocido de 973 milímetros de largo y 381 milímetros circunferencia, AMNH 680 podría haber superado una masa de 2.65 t y haber alcanzado una longitud superior a 9 metros, hasta 9,7 metros

facts.statement: The proposed weight range for the genus Allosaurus has varied between 1,000 and 4,000 kilograms across all specimens.
facts.quote: El rango de peso propuesto para el género ha variado entre 1000 a 4000 kilogramos, teniendo en cuenta todos los especímenes

facts.statement: It is debated how many valid species of Allosaurus exist, as the number depends on the author.
facts.quote: el número de especies válidas es dudoso y depende del autor

facts.statement: Species such as Allosaurus europaeus, Allosaurus jimmadseni, and Allosaurus lucasi have been proposed but are disputed by researchers.
facts.quote: En 2006 en Portugal se describió Allosaurus europaeus, aunque solo fue separada tentativamente dada la localización geográfica y Allosaurus jimmadseni de EE.UU. y la tercera especie de este último país, Allosaurus lucasi, en 2014. Sin embargo, todas ellas han sido disputadas

facts.statement: Recent studies support the hypothesis that some large specimens historically referred to Allosaurus belong to separate genera.
facts.quote: recientes estudios apoyan la hipótesis de dos géneros separados

facts.statement: The skull and teeth of Allosaurus were modest in size compared to other theropods of its body size.
facts.quote: El cráneo y los dientes de Allosaurus tenían un tamaño modesto si lo comparamos con otros terópodos de su tamaño.

facts.statement: Allosaurus presents a paradox of having a strong skull but a relatively weak bite force.
facts.quote: un cráneo fuerte con una mordida débil

facts.statement: Paleontologist Gregory S. Paul estimated a skull size of 845 mm for an individual measuring 7.9 meters in length.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul ha estimado un tamaño de 845 milímetros para el cráneo de un individuo de 7,9 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Each premaxilla bone at the tip of the snout possessed five teeth with a D-shaped cross-section.
facts.quote: Cada premaxilar, los huesos que forman la punta del hocico, tenían cinco dientes con una sección al corte con forma de D

facts.statement: The dentary bone supporting the lower jaw teeth contained between 14 and 17 teeth, averaging 16.
facts.quote: Cada dentario, el hueso que soporta los dientes de la mandíbula inferior tenían entre 14 y 17 dientes, con un promedio de 16.

facts.statement: All teeth possessed serrated edges.
facts.quote: Todos los dientes tenía bordes aserrados.

facts.statement: The teeth were easily lost and continuously replaced, making them the most common fossils found.
facts.quote: Estos se perdían con facilidad, y fueron reemplazados continuamente, por lo que son los fósiles más comunes.

facts.statement: Unlike other theropods, allosaurs had a pair of blunt, horn-like bumps formed by extensions of the lacrimal bone and two parallel lines of small bony bumps on the nasal bone.
facts.quote: A diferencia de otros terópodos, los alósauridos tenían un par de abultamientos, similares a "cuernos" embotados, formados por extensiones del hueso lagrimal y dos líneas paralelas de pequeñas protuberancias óseas sobre el hueso nasal

facts.statement: It is debated whether the head ornamentations served to protect eyes from the sun, for display, or for intraspecific combat, despite being very fragile.
facts.quote: Se ha argumentado que poseían gran variedad de funciones, incluyendo que funcionaban para proteger del sol los ojos, para exhibiciones, y para combates entre individuos de la misma especies aunque eran muy frágiles.

facts.statement: Depressions within the lacrimal bones were present to contain a gland similar to a salt gland.
facts.quote: Dentro de los huesos lacrimales tenía unas depresiones para contener una glándula, similar a la glándula de sal.

facts.statement: The thin roof of the skull may have helped improve brain thermoregulation.
facts.quote: El techo del cráneo era fino, quizás para mejorar la termorregulación del cerebro.

facts.statement: Allosaurus had nine cervical vertebrae, 14 dorsal vertebrae, and five sacral vertebrae supporting the pelvis.
facts.quote: Allosaurus tenía nueve vértebras en el cuello, 14 en la espalda, y cinco en el sacro donde apoya la cadera.

facts.statement: The number of tail vertebrae is unknown, with James Madsen estimating around 50 and Gregory S. Paul suggesting 45 or fewer.
facts.quote: James Madsen estima alrededor de 50, mientras que Gregory S. Paul considera que este número es demasiado alto y sugirió 45 o menos.

facts.statement: Hollow spaces were present in the cervical and anterior dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: En las vértebras del cuello y la porción anterior de la espalda había espacios huecos.

facts.statement: These hollow spaces are interpreted as being occupied by air sacs used for respiration, a feature also found in modern birds.
facts.quote: Estos espacios, que se encuentran también en los terópodos modernos, es decir, las aves, son interpretados como ocupados por los sacos aéreos que se usan en la respiración.

facts.statement: The rib cage was wide, giving the chest a barrel shape, particularly compared to less derived theropods like Ceratosaurus.
facts.quote: La caja costal era amplia, dándole un pecho con forma de barril, especialmente con respecto a los menos derivados terópodos como Ceratosaurus.

facts.statement: In a published case, gastralia (abdominal ribs) showed injuries sustained during the animal's life.
facts.quote: En un caso publicado, las gastralias muestran lesiones durante la vida.

facts.statement: The ilium was large and strong, while the pubis had a prominent projection that may have served for muscle insertion and for leaning the body against the ground.
facts.quote: El ilion, el hueso principal de la cadera, era grande y fuerte, y el pubis tenía un saliente prominente que se pudo haber utilizado para la inserción de músculos y como apoyo para reclinar el cuerpo en la tierra.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that the lack of fusion in the pubis of some individuals is a sexual characteristic aiding egg-laying, though this proposal has not gained scientific attention.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que esto es una característica sexual, donde las hembra carecieron de la fusión para poder poner los huevos más fácilmente. Esta propuesta no ha atraído la atención del medio científico.

facts.statement: Although the forelimbs were short compared to the hindlimbs, they were massive and possessed eagle-like claws.
facts.quote: A pesar de que los miembros delanteros eran cortos en comparación a los miembros traseros, estos eran masivos y con garras parecidas a las del águila.

facts.statement: The arms of allosaurs were short compared to their hind legs, measuring only 35% of the hind leg length in an adult specimen.
facts.quote: Los brazos de los alosaurios eran cortos en comparación a sus patas traseras, solo el 35% del largo de estas en un ejemplar adulto.

facts.statement: The hands had three fingers ending in large, strong, and curved claws.
facts.quote: Teniendo tres dedos por mano, terminados en unas garras, grandes y fuertes y curvadas.

facts.statement: The wrist possessed a version of the semilunar bone found in more derived theropods such as maniraptorans.
facts.quote: Este tenía una versión del hueso semilunar en el carpo cosa encontrada en los terópodos más derivados como en los maniraptores.

facts.statement: Each foot had three strong toes contacting the ground and one spur-like toe that Madsen suggested could be used to grasp young prey.
facts.quote: Cada pie tenía tres fuertes dedos que contactaban el piso y uno, como un garrón que Madsen sugirió se habría podido utilizase para agarrar en los jóvenes.

facts.statement: Allosaurus belongs to the parent group Allosauroidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Allosauroidea

facts.statement: Allosaurus is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Allosaurus lived from the Oxfordian to the Berriasian stages, between 161.5 and 137.05 million years ago.
